blocks.x: COM SKILLS 157 · Communication Skills · Topic 2

Good communication depends on a hearer or reader being able to arrive at only one sensible meaning. When a word, phrase or sentence can reasonably carry more than one meaning, communication breaks down — this topic maps out where that uncertainty comes from and how to write around it.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Define ambiguity and explain, with the Greek root ambiguus ("uncertain"), why a word, phrase, clause or sentence is called ambiguous when it can reasonably be read in more than one way.
2Distinguish intentional from unintentional ambiguity, and recognise deliberate ambiguity as a device used in advertising and literature.
3Explain lexical ambiguity and tell apart its two causes — phonological ambiguity (homophones) and semantic ambiguity (homonyms) — with examples.
4Identify all six sources of structural (syntactic) ambiguity in a sentence and state both possible readings each one produces.
5Define misrelated constructions, apply the grammatical principle that governs opening phrases, and correct misrelated sentences by moving or introducing the subject.

6Recognise the three exception categories — absolute constructions, sentence adverbials, and participial phrases functioning as prepositions/conjunctions — that are acceptable even though they look "misrelated."

blocks.x: Key definitions

Ambiguity From the Greek word ambiguus, meaning uncertain. Ambiguity is uncertainty in meaning: a word, a phrase, a clause or a sentence is ambiguous if it can reasonably be interpreted in more than one way. (Afreh, 2024)

Intentional ambiguity Ambiguity created deliberately, often for stylistic or persuasive effect. It is common in advertisements and literature: • "I like the sprite in you." (advertisement) — is it the soft drink Sprite, or the spirit in you? • "Thou still unravished bride of quietness…" — John Keats, "Ode on a Grecian Urn" — does still mean "unmoving/motionless," or "not yet changed"?

Unintentional ambiguity The unconscious use of ambiguous expressions — the writer or speaker is simply unclear or inexact without meaning to be. This is the kind of ambiguity that good writers actively try to eliminate, and it is the main focus of the rest of this topic.
Ambiguity→ Lexical (Phonological / Semantic)→ Structural (6 sources)→ Misrelated Constructions→ Corrections & Exceptions
Ambiguity at the level of the word

Lexical ambiguity is ambiguity at the level of the lexical items of a language — the confusion is caused by the word itself, before it is even combined into a phrase or sentence. It has two distinct causes: sound and form.

Lexical ambiguity Ambiguity that arises from a single word having more than one possible meaning, independent of sentence structure. It splits into two types: phonological ambiguity (caused by homophones) and semantic ambiguity (caused by homonyms).
Phonological ambiguity (homophones)
Caused by homophones: words that have the same pronunciation but a different spelling and meaning. Heard aloud, without any spelling to disambiguate them, these words are indistinguishable.
Homophone pair
I / eye
Homophone pair
write / right
Homophone pair
flower / flour
Homophone pair
nose / knows
Homophone pair
hear / here
Semantic ambiguity (homonyms)

Caused by homonyms: words that share the same form/spelling and the same pronunciation, but carry different meanings depending on the context in which they are used. Unlike homophones, homonyms cannot be told apart even in writing — only context resolves them.
Homonym
bank — a financial institution, or the bank/edge of a river.
Homonym
tie — a necktie worn around the neck, or a drawn/level score in a contest.
Homonym
watch — a wristwatch that tells the time, or the act of watching/observing something.
Homonym
letter — a written/posted message, or a letter of the alphabet.

blocks.title: Phonological vs. semantic ambiguity — what's the real difference?

items: Phonological ambiguity (homophones): different spelling, same sound — e.g. flower vs flour. The ambiguity mainly shows up in speech, since the spelling would disambiguate it in writing.
Semantic ambiguity (homonyms): same spelling and same sound — e.g. bank (money) vs bank (river). The ambiguity persists in both speech and writing, and only the surrounding context can resolve it.
Both are forms of lexical ambiguity because the confusion lives in the individual word, not in how the sentence is built.

sections.title: Wrong or careless ordering of words

blocks.x: Ambiguity built into sentence structure

Structural ambiguity results from putting words together as structures — phrases, clauses or sentences — in a way that supports more than one grammatical reading. Because it is ambiguity in syntax, it is also called syntactic ambiguity. There are six recognised sources.

Structural ambiguity Ambiguity that arises not from any single word, but from how words are arranged into a phrase, clause or sentence — the individual words may each be perfectly clear, yet the combination allows two different grammatical structures (and therefore two different meanings).
Wrong or careless ordering of words

items: AExample: "The minister decided to appoint a panel of independent doctors to examine his deputy on August 31." The string "on August 31" is meant to give the time of some action or event — but which one? Is it the time the minister decided, the time he appointed the panel, or the time the panel is to examine his deputy? Careless placement of the time phrase at the very end leaves all three readings open.

blocks.x: Unclear modification

items: B"The Vice-Chancellor has refused to enter dirty students' halls." Does dirty modify the halls (the halls are dirty) or, by loose association, describe the students themselves as dirty? The modifier's target is unclear.

B"The hall master has decided against attending anymore boring students' hall week celebrations." Is it the celebrations that are boring, or is boring loosely describing the students' hall week in a way that could be read either way?

B"He ate the meal on the couch." Was the meal on the couch (an odd place for food), or did he sit on the couch while eating? The prepositional phrase "on the couch" can attach to either "the meal" or the act of eating.

B"Visiting friends can be boring." Is it boring to visit friends (friends being visited), or are friends who are visiting you the boring ones? "Visiting" can be read as a gerund (the act of visiting) or a participle modifying "friends."

blocks.x: Ambiguous reference (especially with pronouns)

items: C"Take the items from the boxes and wash them." Does them refer to the items, or to the boxes? The pronoun could point back to either noun.
C"When I tried to glue the handle onto the cup, it broke." Did the handle break, or did the cup break? "It" has two possible antecedents.
C"Mansa told her that she is next on the programme." Is Mansa next on the programme, or is the other woman (her/she) next? With two female referents in play, "she" is ambiguous.

blocks.x: Ambiguous word or phrase in a sentence

items: D"The shooting of the policeman angered the people." Did the policeman shoot someone (policeman as the doer), or was the policeman shot (policeman as the victim)? The phrase "shooting of the policeman" supports both a subjective and an objective reading.
D"The killing of the lady infuriated the family." Did the lady kill someone, or was the lady killed? Same subjective/objective ambiguity as above.
D"The arrest of the lady infuriated the family." Did the lady arrest someone, or was the lady arrested? The "of" phrase again leaves the doer/receiver of the action unclear.

blocks.x: A negative statement followed immediately by a clause of reason

items: E"I didn't give Ode the money because she is a student." — negative statement + reason clause. This can mean either: (a) I did give Ode the money, but not for the reason stated (i.e. not because she's a student — some other reason); or (b) I did not give Ode the money, and the reason I withheld it is precisely that she is a student.

E"I do not like him because he is clever." — same pattern. This can mean either: (a) I do like him, but not because he is clever (I like him for some other reason); or (b) I do not like him, and the reason is that he is clever.

blocks.x: Wrong placement of frequency adverbs

items: FRule: Frequency adverbs — such as frequently, usually, always and normally — should be placed before the main verb. Placed elsewhere, they render the sentence ambiguous. Ambiguous *"Josephine doesn't eat breakfast normally." — does "normally" describe how she eats breakfast (i.e. not in the normal manner) when she does eat it, or does it describe how often she skips it? Clear "Josephine doesn't normally eat breakfast." — placing "normally" before the verb "eat" makes only one reading possible: she does not usually eat breakfast.

blocks.title: Quick self-check: which source of structural ambiguity is at work?

items: A pronoun like it, her or them could point to two different nouns → Source C, ambiguous reference.
A time/place phrase is tacked on the end and could apply to more than one verb in the sentence → Source A, wrong/careless word ordering.
An "X of Y" phrase leaves it unclear whether Y did the action or received it → Source D, ambiguous word or phrase.
An adjective or participle could describe more than one noun in the sentence → Source B, unclear modification.
"Not" + a "because" clause together could mean two opposite things → Source E, negative statement + reason clause.
Frequently, usually, always or normally sits after the verb instead of before it → Source F, wrong placement of a frequency adverb.

blocks.x: When modifiers attach to the wrong noun

A misrelated construction is a special, very common case of structural ambiguity — and outright faulty grammar — in which an opening modifying phrase ends up describing the wrong noun in the sentence, sometimes producing an unintentionally comic reading.

Misrelated construction Occurs when modifiers are attached to constructions they (the modifiers) are not supposed to qualify. Typically an opening participial or infinitive phrase ends up describing the wrong noun that follows it, instead of the noun the writer actually meant.
Spot the misrelation

items: 1"Having been written, Leslie posted the letter." — grammatically, it is Leslie who has "been written," not the letter.
2"When sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt." — grammatically, it is "the next step" that is "sufficiently cooked," which makes no sense.
3"While walking, his feet hit a stone." — grammatically, it is "his feet" that were "walking," not the person.
4"When angry, one's pulse rate quickens." — grammatically, it is "one's pulse rate" that is "angry," not the person whose pulse it is.
5"Trying desperately to think of an excuse, Naa's poor heart pounded against her ribs." — grammatically, it is "Naa's poor heart" that is "trying to think of an excuse," not Naa herself.

blocks.x: The grammatical principle

The grammatical principle Opening phrases such as the ones above should, with certain exceptions (covered in the next tab), relate to the first noun, pronoun or other noun-equivalent that follows them.

head: Opening phrase
Grammatically relates to (first noun/pronoun that follows)

c: Trying desperately to think of an excuse

blocks.x: In every case above, the noun that grammatically follows the opening phrase is not what the writer intended it to describe — there is a conflict between the grammatical requirement and the intended meaning. This conflict is exactly what makes a construction "misrelated."
Two sources of misrelated constructions
Source A

Omission of subjects. The sentence never states who or what the opening phrase truly belongs to, so it latches onto whatever noun happens to come next. "When sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt." — Question: when what is sufficiently cooked? The subject (the food) was never named. "While walking, his feet hit a stone." — Question: who was walking? The person doing the walking was omitted, leaving only "his feet."
Source B

Misplacement of the subject. The true subject of the opening phrase is present in the sentence, but it is placed in the wrong position — after some other noun has already taken the "first noun" slot. "Having been written, Leslie posted the letter." — the true subject of "having been written" is the letter, but "Leslie" occupies the first-noun position instead. Compare: "Having been written, the letter was posted by Leslie." — here the subject is correctly placed.

blocks.title: Why misrelated constructions matter for clear writing

items: They are a leading cause of unintentionally comic or nonsensical sentences in student and professional writing (a "pounding heart" that is "trying to think of an excuse," feet that go "walking" on their own).
They are graded as grammatical errors, not just style issues, because they violate the rule that an opening phrase must relate to the first noun/pronoun that follows it.
The next tab covers exactly how to correct them, and the important exceptions where an apparently "misrelated" opening phrase is in fact perfectly acceptable.

blocks.x: Fixing the fault — and knowing when it isn't one

Once a misrelated construction is identified, the remedy depends on which of the two sources produced it. But not every "opening phrase + different subject" pattern is wrong — three whole categories of construction are exceptions to the rule.
Correcting misrelated constructions
Strategy 1 — Move the subject
Whenever there is a misplacement of the subject (the true subject exists in the sentence but is in the wrong place), move it into the position right after the opening phrase.
Before "Having been written, Leslie posted the letter." After "Having been written, the letter was posted by Leslie."
Strategy 2 — Introduce the missing subject
Whenever there is an omission of the subject (no true subject was ever stated), name the missing subject explicitly inside or right after the opening phrase.
Before "When sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt." After "When the meat/fish/rice is sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt."
Before "While walking, his feet hit a stone." After "While Kofi was walking, he hit his feet against a stone" (or, equivalently, "While walking, he hit his feet against a stone.")
Exceptions to the rule

Some opening phrases look, on the surface, exactly like misrelated constructions — but are fully acceptable in standard English because of what kind of phrase they are. There are three recognised exception categories.
Exception A
Absolute constructions

Phrases that carry their own subject, so they are grammatically complete on their own and do not need to attach to the sentence's main noun. "That said / That being the case, we can leave now." "All things considered, he's very honest."
Exception B
Sentence adverbials

Constructions that function like an adverb for the whole sentence — they comment on the main sentence or link it to other sentences, rather than describing a noun. "Speaking frankly, he's very honest." · "To be frank, he's very honest." · "Simply stated, he's very honest." · "To sum up, he's very honest."
Exception C
Participial phrases as prepositions/conjunctions

Participial phrases that have, over time, become fixed prepositions or conjunctions in English, and so no longer need to relate to the following noun. "Considering his age, he's very fit." · "Considering that he's 66, he's very fit." · "According to the doctor, he's very fit."
Other acceptable "apparently misrelated" constructions
Beyond the three categories above, a further set of fixed expressions are fully acceptable in standard usage even though they appear, at first glance, to be misrelated:

Acceptable fixed expressions
owing to • provided that • regarding • concerning • allowing for • broadly speaking • strictly speaking • putting two and two together • putting it simply • taking everything into account • using the term loosely • coming down to details • assuming • supposing • granting/granted • depending on • excluding • perhaps • come to think of it • come to that

blocks.title: Practice: is it misrelated, or an accepted exception?

items: "He showed the painting to the customer with large patterns." — misrelated/ambiguous modification: "with large patterns" should describe the painting, not sit next to "customer." Rewrite: "He showed the customer the painting with large patterns."

"Feeling hot and thirsty, the fresh coconut milk tasted very good indeed." — misrelated: it is the coconut milk, not a person, that grammatically "feels hot and thirsty." Rewrite: "Feeling hot and thirsty, she found the fresh coconut milk tasted very good indeed."

"Encouraged by high grades, working even harder seemed to make a lot of sense." — misrelated: "working" cannot be "encouraged by high grades" in the intended sense; the missing human subject needs to be introduced.
"The man on the horse with the wide-brimmed hat was the one who told me." — unclear modification: does the horse or the man wear the wide-brimmed hat? Rewrite to attach the hat clearly to the man.

"Once mixed thoroughly, you must shape the concrete before it hardens." — misrelated: "you" did not get "mixed thoroughly" — the concrete did. Rewrite: "Once the concrete is mixed thoroughly, you must shape it before it hardens."
"Although only a small girl, my mother expected me to do a lot of work." — misrelated: it is "I," not "my mother," who was "only a small girl."
"Writing desk for sale by a lady with Queen Anne legs." — unclear modification (and unintentionally comic): "with Queen Anne legs" should describe the desk, not the lady selling it.
"Considering his age, he's very fit." — not misrelated: "Considering" here functions as a preposition (Exception C), so it does not need to relate to "he."
